key_claims.claim: Discovery: house found ~8:30 a.m. Monday June 10 by Ross R. Moore and Mrs. Mary E. Peckham, who were first to enter (contradicts the later 7:00-7:30 a.m. accounts)
key_claims.quote: In 'such condition was the house found at about half past oight [sic] o'clock Monday morning by Ross R. Moore and Mrs. Mary E. Peckham, who were first, to enter and to look upon the terrible scene, so far as the downstairs portion of the house contributed to it.

key_claims.claim: Peckham's sworn inquest testimony: lived next door west on East Third St., ~20 ft away; saw family before church time, not after; curtains down, door locked, called Ross Moore (inquest, Tuesday June 11, 1912)
key_claims.quote: Mrs. Peckham stated that she had been acquainted with J. B. Moore and his family for more than thirteen years, living just next door west of them on East Third street. The distance between the two houses is not more than twenty feet, she thought.

key_claims.claim: Peckham testified she retired ~8 p.m., arose between four and five o'clock Monday, and became alarmed toward eight o'clock at the 'terrible stillness' and the curtained house
key_claims.quote: She retired about eight o'clock, not feeling well, and arose Monday morning between Hour [four] and f\ye [five] o'clock and started to do a washing. Along toward eight o'clock she felt conscious of a terrible stillness around the Moore home

key_claims.claim: Peckham phoned Ross Moore's residence after finding the door locked; also called Ed Selley at the Moore store
key_claims.quote: Mrs. Peckham returned home and called up Ross Moore's residence, and asked Mrs. Moore if there was anything the matter down to the C. C. Moore home, or if Father Moore was sick

key_claims.claim: City Marshal J. H. Horton was first to go upstairs, accompanied by Dr. J. C. Cooper and Dr. E. C. Hough
key_claims.quote: Not until Marshal J. H. Horton appeared upon the scene did any one attempt to go upstairs, and then the marshal, in company with Dr. J. C. Cooper and Dr. E. C. Hough, came upon the fullness of the awful tragedy

key_claims.claim: Children's Day: the Moore children 'had taken prominent parts in the Children's Day exercises' the evening they died (Presbyterian church)
key_claims.quote: Their children, like the parents, were ever ready to take a part in Sunday school work and the evening preceding their death had taken prominent parts in the Children's Day exercises.

key_claims.claim: Crime scene: Stillinger girls downstairs with heads 'chopped open with an ax'; Moores upstairs on their backs 'apparently as they were when asleep'; no signs of struggle except a slight cut on one downstairs girl's arm
key_claims.quote: There were no signs of a struggle on the part of any of the victims, except perhaps in the case of one of the girls downstairs, on whose arm a slight cut appeared.

key_claims.claim: Scene condition: all curtains pulled down and doors darkened with an old black apron and a black skirt; mirrors draped (per later trial summary)
key_claims.quote: he had taken the precaution to pull down all the window curtains and to darken the doors, using an old black apron in one case and a black skirt in the other.

key_claims.claim: Doors/windows: every door and window locked except the two Stillinger-room windows (shown unused); front dining-room door locked with key missing — theory the murderer took the key
key_claims.quote: Every door and window was locked except the two windows in the room occupied by the Stillinger girls down stairs, and the evidences there showed that they had not been used either in entering or leaving, the house.

key_claims.claim: No robbery: Moore's trousers on the bedpost held keys, three memorandum books, a check from brother G. A. Moore and money; his watch lay on the dresser in the girls' room
key_claims.quote: Robbery was not the motive, for nothing is known [knewn sic] to have been taken from the place. Mr. Moore's trousers hung on the bedpost, and in them were a bunch of keys, three memorandum books, a check drawn by his brother, G. A. Moore, and some money.

key_claims.claim: Lamp evidence: a lamp sat on the floor of the downstairs bedroom; its missing globe was found; fingerprints on globe and ax to be used for identification
key_claims.quote: upon receiving a special permit to enter [enfer sic] the Moore home here, found the missing [missings sic] globe from the lamp which sat on the floor in the downstairs bedroom. Finger prints on the globe will be used as a means of identification; as will those on the ax found leaning against the wall close to the lamp.

key_claims.claim: Time-of-death window data point: Mrs. F. F. Jones heard a peculiar noise and had her husband turn on a light between one and two o'clock that night
key_claims.quote: Mrs. F. F. Jones thought she heard a peculiar noise in the vicinity of her home, and had Mr. Jones get up and turn on a light. This was between one and two o'clock.

key_claims.claim: Coroner's inquest opened Tuesday June 11, 1912, 1:30 p.m. at the city hall; eleven witnesses by 3:30 p.m.; coroner A. L. Linquist of Stanton; jury Lomas, Finlayson, Wickersham; prosecuted by County Attorney W. C. Ratcliff
key_claims.quote: County Coroner A. L Linquist of Stanton, who has been personally in charge of the investigation following the awful tragedy of Sunday night, began an inquest with a jury of three men Tuesday afternoon at half past one o'clock at the city hall, and by half past three had examined eleven witnesses

key_claims.claim: Bodies removed from the Moore home 'Monday night after midnight' by undertakers J. L. Smith and C. N. Fessler; funeral held in the public park Wednesday June 12, 1912 at 3 p.m., bodies lying in caskets at the city hall
key_claims.quote: The bodies of the eight were removed from the J. B. Moore home Monday night after midnight with Undertakers J. L. Smith and C. N. Fessler of Villisca - in charge.

key_claims.claim: Militia posted: Company F under Capt. C. J. Casey ordered out by Sheriff O. E. Jackson; patrol around the Moore home from six o'clock Monday evening
key_claims.quote: Company F under Capt. C. J. Casey was orSered [sic] out by Sheriff O. E. Jackson, and a patrol was staitoned [sic] around the J. B. Moore home at six o'clock Monday evening to keep the curious crowds away

key_claims.claim: Inquest resumed June 18, 1912: J. T. Stillinger recalled, described nervous boarder 'Martin Luther Kellum' (May 15-18, 1912); coroner's jury 'Has Verdict Ready'
key_claims.quote: testified that a man giving the name of "Martin Luther Kellum" came to work for him about Wednesday, May 15 [IS sic], and left Saturday evening, May 18, stating that he thought he would be back.

key_claims.claim: Fingerprint expert M. W. McClaughry (Leavenworth): killer was 'some one thoroughly familiar with the premises' and the two girls downstairs were killed first; photos attempted of the ax and lamp chimney
key_claims.quote: Photographs of the murderer's ax, and of the lamp chimney found under the dresser downstairs, were taken at Mr. McClaughry's request in the hopes that a record might be made of the finger prints thereon, but the prints were not conspicious [sic] enough to be photographed very satisfactorily.

key_claims.claim: State/Burns agency on the case by Sept 1912: Attorney General Cosson employed Burns detective W. S. Gordon (succeeding C. W. Tobie); Gordon and Ratcliff conferred with the governor
key_claims.quote: Attorney General Cosson has again employed a member of the Burns detective agency on the Villisca murder case. The man is W. S. Gordon of Kansas City, and he succeeds C. W. Tobie, who first investigated the case but was subsequently transferred to the Chicago agency.

key_claims.claim: October 1912 Montgomery County grand jury (foreman Walter Sellergren) returned four indictments — none arising from the Moore murders
key_claims.quote: The grand jury, composed of J. E. Parmer of Villisca, S. P. Swanson of Frankfort, J. L Richardson of Red Oak, O. J. Powell of Sherman, W J. Owner, of West, A. O. McQuown of Garfield and Walter Sellergren of Scott, the last named being the foreman, began work immediately and returned four indictments

key_claims.claim: Kelly's first trial (Sept 1917) ended in a hung jury — one holdout juror, T. C. Brown, against acquittal
key_claims.quote: the feeling in Montgomery county has been made worse instead of better by the fact that the jury was "hung" in this manner. Mr. Brown was the last juror accepted. He was seriously objected to by the defense. Rev. Kelly will probably be placed on trial again within a few weeks

key_claims.claim: Kelly acquitted at second trial: 'not guilty' verdict Saturday night (Nov 24, 1917) at half past eight, on the first ballot, after four and a half hours
key_claims.quote: The jury that beard [heard] Kelly's second trial for the Villisca ax murders of 1912 returned a verdict of "not guilty" Saturday night at half past eight o'clock after considering the case four and one-half hours, the jury having retired at four o'clock. The freedom of the minister was decided on the first ballot.

key_claims.claim: Prosecutor's trial characterization of Lena Stillinger's position ('pulled twenty inches down from the head of the bed'... 'work of a pervert') vs later medical conclusion of no sexual assault
key_claims.quote: Lena Stillinger, the oldest female child in the house, who was just budding into charming womanhood, was pulled twenty inches down from the head of the bed. There was a smear of blood on one of her legs. The body was lying on the edge of the bed and the position of the limbs plainly indicated the work of a pervert.

key_claims.claim: Children's Day program ended 9:30 p.m.; family and Stillinger girls walked home, arriving 9:45-10 p.m. (secondary consensus, matches Review's 'church time' testimony)
key_claims.quote: After the program ended at 9:30 p.m., the Moores and the Stillinger sisters walked to the Moores' house, arriving between 9:45 and 10 p.m.

key_claims.claim: Telephone 'all call' ~8:40 a.m. spread news; crowd flooded the house, contaminating the scene; skull fragments taken as souvenirs; weapon handled by hundreds
key_claims.quote: Sometime around 8:40 a.m, the town's central telephone office issued an "all call" alert, advising every household in the town of the murders.

key_claims.claim: Smithsonian: crowd contamination detail (~100 through the house, skull fragments removed) and Linquist's left-handed-swinger determination used against Kelly
key_claims.quote: as many as 100 curious neighbors and townspeople tramped as they pleased through the house, scattering fingerprints, and in one case even removing fragments of Joe Moore's skull as a macabre keepsake.

contradictions: Discovery time: Wikipedia and the 2015 Iowa Legislature PDF say Peckham became concerned at 7:00 a.m.; Iowa Cold Cases says 7:30 a.m.; the contemporaneous Villisca Review says the house 'was found at about half past eight o'clock Monday morning' and Horton was 'called about half past eight'; Peckham's own sworn testimony has her arising 4-5 a.m. and becoming alarmed only 'toward eight o'clock.'

Lena Stillinger's age: 11 per the contemporaneous Villisca Review obituary arithmetic and Wikipedia; 12 per Iowa Cold Cases and the Iowa Legislature PDF ('Lenae, 12'); Smithsonian even says the girls were 'ages 12 and 9' (aging Ina as 9).

Time-of-death window: 'between midnight and 2 a.m.' (Wikipedia) vs 'between midnight and 5 a.m.' (Iowa Legislature PDF); contemporaneous anchor points are Mrs. F. F. Jones's noise heard 'between one and two o'clock' (Review) and the killer leaving 'some time before 5 a.m.' (Smithsonian).

Entry route: 'unlocked back door'/'lifted the latch on the back door' (Iowa Cold Cases, Smithsonian) vs the Review's contemporaneous finding that 'Every door and window was locked except the two windows in the room occupied by the Stillinger girls' (shown unused) and that the murderer probably left by the front door taking the key.

Murder weapon provenance: 'an axe belonging to Josiah' (Wikipedia, Iowa Legislature PDF) vs 'Joe's axe from the back yard' (Iowa Cold Cases) vs 'probably taken from where it had been left in the coal shed' (Smithsonian); the Review says only that the ax was 'found leaning against the wall close to the lamp.'

Bacon from the icebox: 4-lb slab laid next to the axe (Wikipedia, Iowa Cold Cases) vs 'a two-pound slab of uncooked bacon... wrapped in a towel' (Smithsonian); the Review's June 13 front page does not mention it.
Bodies removed: 'Monday night after midnight' (Review, contemporaneous) vs permission given only 'after 10:00 p.m.' and transport complete 'close to 2 a.m.' (Wikipedia).

Inquest start: Review documents sworn testimony before the coroner's jury from 1:30 p.m. Tuesday June 11 with eleven witnesses by 3:30; Wikipedia separately describes the coroner arriving 'later that morning,' the jury convening 'in late afternoon,' and an inquest 'convened June 11.'

Kelly chronology: the prompt's 'arrest June 1913' is unsupported; contemporaneous record shows indictment April 30, 1917, self-surrender early May 1917, Logan jail, hung jury (first trial, Oct 3, 1917 report), and 'not guilty' verdict Nov 24, 1917 (Nov 28, 1917 issue).

Burns agency timeline: secondary literature frames Burns involvement as beginning in 1916 under J. N. Wilkerson; the Review shows Burns men (C. W. Tobie, then W. S. Gordon) employed by Attorney General Cosson by September 12, 1912.

Whether anyone was indicted in 1912: the October 1912 grand jury returned four indictments, none connected with the Moore murders (Review); the first murder indictment (Kelly) came only April 30, 1917.

Lena Stillinger's resistance/sexual assault: the state argued at Kelly's 1917 trial that the body position 'plainly indicated the work of a pervert'; secondary sources (Wikipedia, Iowa Cold Cases) report doctors found no evidence of sexual abuse.
Stillinger girls' presence: invited by Katherine Moore (Wikipedia, Iowa Legislature PDF) vs the girls themselves 'asked their parents' permission to stay overnight' (Iowa Cold Cases).
